pr_title: Change assign_attributes to assign the association's _id first. Fixes…
pr_body:
[Fix #52791]

### Motivation / Background

Addresses the use case where if an association's _id is later in the params than the association's _attributes, the nested attributes will not be applied.

This Pull Request has been created because the upgrade from 7.1.3.4. to 7.2.1 caused tests in our application to fail. We were assigning the association_id after the association_attributes in our parameters, and due to the order it no longer updated existing models.

issue_context.title: Assigning attributes for nested association raises if association_id is not specified first
issue_context.body:
### Steps to reproduce

In rails 7.1.3.4 specifying the attributes for a nested association would succeed even when the nested association's id was specified after the attributes. That changed with this commit [ded026b] [#49678)

In rails 7.2.0, This broke behavior in our app where an attributes hash was being set on a has_one before the has_one id was set.
I've recreated the order dependency below, and I have a PR forthcoming.

Changing the assign_attributes to first assign all attributes ending with _id prior to assigning other attributes fixes this. A PR with this change is coming with this.

```ruby
# frozen_string_literal: true

require "bundler/inline"

gemfile(true) do
  source "https://rubygems.org"

  gem "rails", "7.2.1"
  # gem "rails", "7.1.3.4"
  gem "sqlite3"
end

require "active_record"
require "minitest/autorun"
require "logger"

# This connection will do for database-independent bug reports.
ActiveRecord::Base.establish_connection(adapter: "sqlite3", database: ":memory:")
ActiveRecord::Base.logger = Logger.new(STDOUT)

ActiveRecord::Schema.define do
  create_table :names, force: true do |t|
    t.string :first_name
  end

  create_table :posts, force: true do |t|
  end

  create_table :authors, force: true do |t|
    t.references :name
    t.references :post
  end
end

class Post < ActiveRecord::Base
  has_many :authors
  accepts_nested_attributes_for :authors
end

class Author < ActiveRecord::Base
  belongs_to :post, optional: true
  belongs_to :name, optional: true
  accepts_nested_attributes_for :name
end

class Name < ActiveRecord::Base
  has_one :author
end

class BugTest < Minitest::Test
  def test_accepts_nested_attributes_with_id_first
    name = Name.create!(first_name: "John")
    post = Post.create!
    attrs = {
      authors_attributes: [{
        name_id: name.id,
        name_attributes: {
          id: name.id,
          first_name: "Jim"
        }
      }]
    }

    post.attributes = attrs
    post.save!

    assert_equal "Jim", post.authors.first.name.first_name
    assert_equal name.id, post.authors.first.name.id
  end

  def test_accepts_nested_attributes_with_id_last
    name = Name.create!(first_name: "John")
    post = Post.create!
    attrs = {
      authors_attributes: [{
        name_attributes: {
          id: name.id,
          first_name: "Jim"
        },
        name_id: name.id
      }]
    }

    post.attributes = attrs
    post.save!

    assert_equal "Jim", post.authors.first.name.first_name
    assert_equal name.id, post.authors.first.name.id
  end
end

```

### Expected behavior
Expected that the model saves with no problems.

### Actual behavior
Recieved an RecordNotFound raised

### System configuration
**Rails version**: 7.2.1

**Ruby version**: 3.3.4

review_comments:
I think nested parameters should come after multi parameters. It probably does not matter much since the important detail is to assign foreign key values before nested parameters. I wonder if it is possible to have a foreign key needing a multi parameter attribute?
Anyway, simple solution
```suggestion
        assign_multiparameter_attributes(multi_parameter_attributes) if multi_parameter_attributes
        assign_nested_parameter_attributes(nested_parameter_attributes) if nested_parameter_attributes
```

I'm not convinced we should be changing anything without a failing test showing why its necessary to change. The previous order was there for 4 years and I haven't seen any issues reported with it.

This PR exists because the Active Record test suite was lacking coverage. What if changing the order is also not covered but some app breaks by changing it?

Ok, reverting back the original commit of just adding the test.

If the order as mentioned above should change and needs a test to drive it, it probably belongs in a different PR with a different issue to drive the change. Keeping this scoped to just the bug fix that the original code removal changed is probably most appropriate.

I could add a test to drive the change in this PR if needed, or I could change this to deal with multiparameter foreign key in a different PR. To me, it makes little difference, I only want to get whatever can get this issue fixed the quickest. My main focus is not having the issue popping up in our local app.
